did_you_know.text: Psalm 92 opens with the heading “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day,” presenting the Sabbath from the very beginning as a central part of the psalm’s theme.
The verse emphasizes that giving thanks to the Lord and singing praises to His name are “good”—that is, worthy and joyful acts.
The psalm describes a cycle of day and night: in the morning, people proclaim the Lord’s lovingkindness, and at night, His faithfulness.

Several musical instruments are mentioned in the psalm: the ten-stringed instrument, the lute, and the lyre, along with musical accompaniment on the lyre. Prayer is therefore presented as singing accompanied by instruments.
The psalmist’s joy comes from the Lord’s works: “For You have made me glad by Your deeds; I sing for joy over the works of Your hands.”
The psalmist marvels at the greatness of the Lord’s works and the depth of His thoughts, noting that a foolish person does not understand them.
The flourishing of the wicked is compared to grass that grows quickly. According to the psalm, their success is not lasting and ultimately ends in destruction.
The psalmist uses two images of strength and renewal: “You have exalted my horn like that of a wild ox,” and “I am anointed with fresh oil.”
The righteous are compared to two strong, flourishing trees: the palm tree and the cedar of Lebanon. These images express growth and stability.

The righteous are described as planted in the house of the Lord and in the courts of their God. They continue to bear fruit even in old age, and the psalm concludes by connecting this testimony to the Lord’s uprightness and the fact that there is no injustice in Him.
